build.pitch: Build a 5-question 'golden answer' eval and score how often the model actually gets them right — ATLAS's grading method, shrunk to one file.
build.why: Riffs on today's ATLAS benchmark item (search agents missing the 'golden' answer on real tasks) — strip away the web-search part and you're left with the core eval pattern underneath: a fixed answer key plus a scorer that decides hit or miss. Building that pattern yourself is the fastest way to feel how much of 'evaluating an agent' is really about writing a good answer key.

plan.step: Write 5 trivia-style questions with known, unambiguous short answers (facts, not opinions or anything web-search-dependent) — your answer key.
Send each question to Claude Haiku 5.5 via the Messages API, one at a time, collecting the plain-text responses.
Write a ~10-line scorer: normalize case/whitespace, check exact match plus a looser 'does the golden answer appear in the response' check, mark each question hit or miss.
Print a scorecard — each question with its hit/miss, and a final 'X/5' — and eyeball any miss: was the model actually wrong, or was your question ambiguous?

build.done_looks_like: Running the script prints 5 rows, each marked hit or miss, plus a final score like '4/5' — and for any miss you can tell from the printed answer whether the model got it wrong or your question was the problem.
build.stretch_goal: Add a second, harder question set that needs a bit of multi-step reasoning instead of pure recall, and compare hit rates between the two sets — a toy version of ATLAS's difficulty tiers.

reading.intro: Latent Space was the busy one today — three separate posts landed in the window: two long-form interviews (industrial robotics, AI-for-biology) plus the AINews digest recapping the last 24h of AI Twitter/X. Towards Data Science's regular digest also had one fresh piece worth pulling out. TLDR AI's usual morning edition hadn't landed yet as of brief time, and Morning Brew, The New Stack, Rundown, DeepLearning.AI, and Import AI were all stale or off-topic for the window. The AINews digest is Twitter-recap style — short claims attributed to named accounts rather than full articles — so a few items below carry a couldn't-independently-verify-the-exact-numbers caveat; treat those as directional, not gospel.

items.title: Inside Standard Bots' AI stack: pretrained models, zero-shot perception, and why targeted data beats big data
items.why: America's largest AI-native industrial robot manufacturer (NASA, Amazon, and Lockheed Martin are customers) explains its actual production stack: a shared base model adapted per customer through demonstrations, a zero-shot perception model trained on a billion+ images, motion handled by conventional code, training in the cloud but inference always local. The 'co-optimize model and hardware' and 'targeted data beats bigger data' arguments apply just as well to software agents.

items.title: Why AlphaFold Didn't Solve Protein Folding
items.why: Google DeepMind's Pushmeet Kohli (AlphaFold) and Biohub's Sal Candido on what the 'protein folding is solved' headline glosses over: AlphaFold reproduces a static structure deposited in the PDB, not the real distribution of shapes a protein can take, and dynamics, disorder, and design are still wide open. A concrete case study in the 'bitter lesson for data' — sometimes the right move is more data, sometimes more inductive bias, and knowing which is the actual skill.

items.title: Decision models become a product category overnight
items.why: In the space of one day, OpenAI (Decisions API), Microsoft (Decision-1), Perplexity (pplx-decider-v1.1), Cloudflare (clef), and Liquid (d1) all shipped models that return a typed answer — a probability, a pick from a list, a score — in one forward pass instead of free text. The pitch: most agent steps are a yes/no or a pick-one, not a generation, so a dedicated 'decision' call is faster and cheaper than a full chat completion. LangChain says routing to the cheapest adequate model this way cut median cost per coding task by 64%.

items.title: Do multi-agent 'teams' actually pay off? A coding benchmark says mostly no
items.source: Latent Space (AINews digest, citing a Vals AI study)
items.why: Vals AI reportedly ran GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 solo versus as agent 'teams' on a coding benchmark: teams cost 1.8–5.1x more in tokens, and only one configuration (Sol at medium reasoning effort) improved meaningfully. Opus ran roughly 6.8 subagents and ~1,140 subagent tool calls per app at max effort for no measurable gain. We couldn't find Vals' own report to confirm the exact figures independently — treat the numbers as reported, not verified — but the shape of the finding (coordination overhead often outweighing parallelism) matches other recent multi-agent benchmarking.

items.title: Claude agents can now fan out into 1,000-agent workflows
items.why: A newly flagged capability on Claude's managed-agents stack: a lead agent writes a phased plan, fans it out to up to 1,000 subagents per run, then merges the results, enabled via a new API header. Anthropic's own guidance warns to start with narrowly scoped tasks since token use (and cost) scales fast. Worth reading next to the item above — raw fan-out capacity and 'does it actually help' are two very different questions right now.

items.title: Gemini 4 Argon reportedly beats Opus 5.5 on a coding benchmark — but almost nobody can use it yet
items.why: Google says Argon scores 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1 versus Opus 5.5's 74.2% (Opus still wins Terminal-bench 4.0). The catch: Argon ships first to roughly 650 government, cloud, and cybersecurity 'Fairwind Program' partners, not the general API or app — so for most people this is a benchmark screenshot, not a model you can touch yet.

items.title: Prime Intellect's open-source, self-improving coding agent keeps leveling up
items.source: Open Source For You, via Latent Space AINews
items.why: Prime Agent, Prime Intellect's MIT-licensed coding harness, can inspect its own execution history and patch its prompts, subagents, and memory via a /refine command (its core system prompt stays fixed). It already scores 95.5% on ARC-AGI-3 paired with Opus 5, edging the reported 95.4% human-expert baseline. Today's AINews digest references further swarm-scale Rust work we couldn't independently verify — worth watching for a primary write-up before taking that number at face value.

items.title: Stop Using AI. Start Hiring It.
items.why: Gursimar Singh's framing: the mistake isn't using AI, it's using it like a loose tool instead of managing it like hired help — with onboarding, scoped responsibility, and performance review. Simple reframe, but a decent gut-check if your own AI workflows are all ad hoc prompts with no structure around them.

build.pitch: Build a tiny 'decision vs. chat' harness and watch how much parsing it takes just to turn free text into a yes/no.
build.why: Riffs on today's 'decision models become a product category overnight' item — the whole pitch for a dedicated decision call (OpenAI, Microsoft, Perplexity, Cloudflare, Liquid all shipped one on the same day) is that most agent steps are a yes/no or pick-one, not a generation. Simulating both paths yourself with canned text makes the parsing tax that free-text answers carry concrete instead of abstract.

plan.step: Write 5 yes/no questions and, for each, a canned 'free-text' answer in a different phrasing ('Yeah, I'd say so.', 'Not really, no.', 'Hard to say, but leaning yes...') — no API key needed.
Write a naive parser that tries to extract yes/no from each free-text answer with simple string checks (startswith, 'yes' in text.lower(), etc.), logging which ones it gets wrong or can't decide.
Write the 'decision mode' equivalent: the same 5 questions, but each answer is just a typed field from a fixed {YES, NO} enum — no parsing step at all.
Print a scoreboard: how many of the 5 free-text answers needed coercion or were ambiguous, versus 0 for decision mode.
